title: Exploring Urological Malignancies on Pinterest: Content Analysis
screen_reason: Content analysis of 359 English-language Pinterest pins retrieved by four cancer search terms. Two reviewers independently scored every pin for the presence of misinformation on a published 1 (none) to 5 (high) Likert scale, and Table 1 reports the share of pins scoring >1 for each cancer with counts and denominators (bladder 16/61 = 26%, kidney 9/100 = 9%, prostate 15/98 = 15%, testicular 4/100 = 4%). These are shares of items judged for factual accuracy with stated denominators -> CONTENT. The DISCERN and PEMAT scores are QUALITY.

The reviewers are the (urology) author team. estimates.notes: breadth coded 'misleading' (the broadest band) because the numerator is any pin scoring above the floor of a 5-point misinformation scale, a permissive threshold that will capture partially misleading as well as flatly false content. denom_selection curated: the API pull was capped at 540 pins across four terms (135 per term before exclusions), so the corpus is rank/count-truncated rather than a census. Data-collection date is nowhere stated; year is the publication year. NOTE ON POOLING: no overall misinformation percentage is reported. The Results text gives the same figure: 'Misinformation ranged from 4% (n=4) in testicular cancer to 26% (n=16) in bladder cancer pins'.

estimates.notes: QUALITY row per INSTRUCTIONS section 3 (DISCERN -> QUALITY), kept for the appendix and excluded from prevalence: a factually accurate pin scores <=3 on DISCERN whenever it omits sources, risks or alternatives. THE PAPER'S OWN PERCENTAGE IS WRONG: the count 298 is exactly the sum of Table 1's per-cancer counts (50+87+94+67), and 298/359 = 83.0%, not 'nearly 75%'. I kept the verbatim 75% under R8 rather than substituting my own arithmetic, hence confidence low; an adjudicator should treat 83% as the arithmetically correct figure. This row is not a misinformation prevalence and should not be pooled with the four CONTENT rows. | QUOTE NOTE: source_quote is the contiguous Abstract/Results sentence; the per-cancer breakdown is the contiguous Table 1 row 'Quality score ≤3, n (%) 50 (82) 87 (87) 94 (96) 67 (67)', which is not extracted as separate rows because DISCERN quality is not a falsity share.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) NO POOLED MISINFORMATION FIGURE EXISTS. The abstract gives only the verbatim range 'Misinformative content was apparent in 4%-26% of all genitourinary cancer pins'. Summing Table 1 gives 44/359 = 12.3%, but that is a cross-category sum barred by R8, so I extracted the four per-cancer rows instead. An adjudicator preferring one row per paper should use the 4%-26% range with value_kind range_not_point. (2) PEMAT shares are quality/usability, not accuracy, and were not extracted: 'Understandability and actionability were poor in 55% (n=198) and 100% (n=359) of the pins'. (3) 'Nearly all pins failed to mention shared decision-making (n=348, 97%)' is a completeness measure. (4) Commercial bias counts (bladder 4 (7%), kidney 1 (1%), prostate 14 (14%), testicular 0 (0%)) measure paid endorsement, not falsity. (5) Racial/ethnic representation shares (86% White, 3% Black among 206 depicted people) are diversity measures. (6) Engagement figures (8,507 total repins; average 25 repins; per-topic follower counts) are dissemination volumes with no misinformation numerator attached, so no EXPOSURE, REACH or CONCENTRATION row is possible - the paper never crosses misinformation with repins. (7) The 28-fold sharing figure for inaccurate urological articles is quoted from Alsyouf et al [12], i.e. a figure the paper cites from elsewhere, which R8 forbids keeping.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. Sampling frame: 540 Pinterest pins pulled through the Pinterest API with four search terms ('bladder cancer', 'kidney cancer', 'prostate cancer', 'testicular cancer'), i.e. 135 per term; exclusions for irrelevance or non-English left 359 pins (bladder 61, kidney 100, prostate 98, testicular 100). No data-collection date is reported anywhere in the paper, and the ranking/ordering rule behind the API pull is not described. Coding: two reviewers independently scored each pin and its linked content on DISCERN (16 items, 1-5), PEMAT (17 items) and a published 1-5 misinformation Likert scale; publisher type and perceived race/ethnicity also coded; interrater discrepancies settled by group discussion. RELIABILITY: no kappa, percentage agreement or any other statistic is reported, although the Limitations section asserts that coding comparisons were performed to verify interrater reliability - so the claim is unverifiable. Authors' limitations: single platform, English only, four most common urological cancers only, validated instruments applied to an interface they were not designed for, subjectivity in scoring, and inability to determine pins' country of origin. ADDITIONAL PROBLEMS FOUND IN THE TEXT: (a) the exclusion rule is stated nonsensically - 'Pins were excluded if they did not contain relevant content (ie, if they did not mention gallbladder or thyroid cancer)' inverts the intended meaning; (b) the abstract's 'Nearly 75% (n=298)' contradicts its own count, since 298/359 = 83.0%; (c) the Results say 'Over 60% (n=198) of bladder, kidney, and prostate cancer pins had low PEMAT scores for understandability', but 198 is the total across ALL FOUR cancers (37+62+69+30) and equals 55%, as the abstract itself states; (d) actionability is given as '100% (n=359)' in the abstract but '99% (n=358)' in the Discussion, and Table 1 sums to 358. None of these touch the four extracted misinformation counts, which are internally consistent (16/61, 9/100, 15/98, 4/100), but they lower confidence in the paper's reporting overall.
